opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important to separate what we actually know from what people assume. There's a common narrative that social media has just destroyed young people's ability to connect, and the data is a bit more nuanced than that, but there are some real effects.

One thing we see as neuroscientists is that the brain is very good at optimizing for whatever environment it's trained in. If you spend your formative years practicing interaction through a screen, where you can edit what you say, take thirty seconds to craft the perfect reply, curate the photo, then you become very skilled at that kind of interaction. But in-person romance is the opposite. It's messy, it's real time, there's no undo button. You have to read a face, tolerate an awkward silence, recover from saying something stupid. And those are skills that, like any skill, weaken if you don't practice them.

So what I hear from a lot of young people is not that they don't want connection. They want it badly. It's that the stakes of the in-person moment feel higher because they've had less rehearsal. The approach at a bar, asking someone out face to face, feels terrifying in a way it maybe didn't for previous generations, because the alternative, swiping, is so low-risk.

And that's the second piece: choice. Dating apps and social media give you the feeling of infinite options. There's a lot of work in decision science showing that when you have too many options, you're less satisfied with whatever you pick, and you're more reluctant to commit, because there's always the sense that someone slightly better is one swipe away. That's not a great mindset for building something deep with one person.

Now, to be fair, there are benefits. People who are in small towns, or who are part of communities that are hard to find, can meet people they never would have met before. Some couples who meet online are doing very well. So it's not that the technology is evil. It's that it changes the training data our brains are getting.

If I had to give advice, it would be pretty simple: treat in-person interaction like a muscle. Go to places where you're forced to talk to people without a screen in between. Accept that it will be awkward at first. The awkwardness isn't a sign that something's wrong with you. It's just the brain learning something it hasn't practiced enough yet.

r001.rationale: It says practicing through a screen can weaken the real-time skills needed for in-person romance, making face-to-face approaches feel more difficult.

r002.rationale: It discusses swiping as low-risk but does not argue that formulaic dating-app greetings fail to generate romantic attraction.

fable-5.1.text:
So I'll give you the neuroscientist's answer first, and then the more honest answer, which is that we don't fully know yet because the experiment is still running on this generation.

The thing about romance, about falling for someone in person, is that it's an enormously high-bandwidth experience. When you sit across from someone, your brain is taking in thousands of signals a second. Pupil dilation, micro-expressions, the pause before they answer a question, the smell, the way they laugh at something that wasn't quite funny. Most of that never reaches your awareness. It gets processed in the background, and what you experience is just a feeling: "I like this person," or "something's off." Your brain is doing the math and only handing you the answer.

Social media compresses all of that into a tiny channel. A profile, a photo, a few lines of text. And here's the problem. When the channel is narrow, the brain doesn't say, "I don't have enough information." It fills in the gaps. It invents the rest of the person. So young people are falling for a version of someone that's maybe twenty percent real data and eighty percent their own projection. And then they meet in person, and the real human arrives with all this noisy, uncontrollable information, and it feels like a disappointment, even when the person is perfectly lovely. The fantasy was easier.

The second thing, and I think this is actually the bigger one, is tolerance for discomfort. Approaching someone in a room is scary. Your heart rate goes up, your amygdala is screaming. That used to be unavoidable. You had to get through it to get what you wanted. Now there's always an exit. You can swipe instead of walking over. You can text instead of calling. Every time you take the exit, you're training the brain that the discomfort was something to avoid rather than something to survive. And the skill of sitting in that awkwardness, which is really the skill of being vulnerable in front of another person, atrophies like any muscle you don't use.

And then there's the comparison problem. The brain evolved to evaluate partners within a village of maybe a hundred and fifty people. Now the apparent pool is infinite, and it's curated. So the person in front of you is always being measured against a thousand highlight reels, and they always lose, because they're real.

Now, the honest part. I talk to a lot of young people, and they're not stupid about this. Many of them know exactly what it's doing to them. There's a kind of exhaustion I see, a hunger for something unmediated. So I'm actually somewhat optimistic. The brain is plastic. These skills come back if you practice them. But you have to choose to walk over to the person in the room, knowing it's going to feel terrible for about thirty seconds. That thirty seconds is the whole thing. That's where the connection lives.

r001.rationale: The response says that swiping and texting can replace approaching or calling in person, training young people to avoid discomfort and weakening the vulnerability skills that support in-person connection.

r002.rationale: It describes social media profiles as a narrow channel, but does not discuss formulaic greetings in dating-app conversations or say they fail to generate romantic attraction.

astra-6.text:
I think social media has made it easier to initiate contact, but it doesn’t necessarily make it easier to be vulnerable. Those are different skills. You can spend an hour crafting a message. In person, there’s a pause, you’re not sure what the other person means, and you have to stay in that uncertainty for a moment.

And that’s part of connecting romantically. You have to let someone see that you’re interested before you know for certain that they’re interested in you. If you get used to communicating in ways where you can edit everything or simply disappear, that moment can feel quite intimidating.

But I wouldn’t say young people have lost the ability. For someone who feels isolated, finding another person online can be an extraordinary opportunity. The question is whether the technology helps you get to a conversation where you can actually know each other, or whether it keeps you endlessly looking for someone else.

r001.rationale: The response says that getting used to editable or easily abandoned messages can make in-person romantic vulnerability intimidating, presenting text-mediated habits as a possible impediment to in-person connection.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss formulaic dating-app greetings or whether they generate romantic attraction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think social media has changed the conditions under which young people learn to connect. Online, you can edit what you say, choose the picture, wait before responding. In person, you don’t have that control. There are pauses, misunderstandings, the possibility of rejection. And becoming comfortable with those things takes practice.

If more of your interaction happens through a screen, you may get less practice at that uncertainty. Then a conversation with someone you’re attracted to can feel unusually difficult, even though the awkwardness is a normal part of it.

But I’d be careful about saying social media simply makes people worse at romance. It also allows people to find each other who might never meet otherwise. The question is whether it helps you move toward a relationship or becomes a place where you can keep avoiding the vulnerability that a relationship requires.

r001.rationale: It says screen-based interaction can mean less practice with in-person uncertainty, making conversation with someone attractive unusually difficult.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss formulaic dating-app greetings or claim they are insufficient to create romantic attraction.
